description: What does [x * 2 for x in [1, 2, 3]] produce?
explanation: A list comprehension applies the expression to each item, giving [2, 4, 6].

description: What does [n for n in range(6) if n % 2 == 0] produce?
explanation: The if clause keeps only items that satisfy it, so only the even numbers 0, 2 and 4 survive.

description: What does {w: len(w) for w in ["hi", "there"]} produce?
explanation: A dictionary comprehension builds keys and values together, mapping each word to its length.
choice3: {"hi", "there"}

description: Which of these types is immutable?
explanation: Tuples cannot be changed after creation. Lists, dictionaries and sets can all be modified in place.
choice3: tuple

description: a = [1, 2] then b = a then b.append(3). What is a now?
explanation: Assignment copies the reference, not the list, so a and b name the same object and both show [1, 2, 3].
hint: Assignment does not copy a list.
choice3: An error is raised

description: How do you make an independent copy of a list named items?
explanation: items[:] or list(items) builds a new list. Plain assignment only creates another name for the same object.
choice3: copy == items

description: Why is a mutable default argument such as def f(x=[]) considered a trap?
explanation: The default is created once when the function is defined, so changes to it persist across every later call.
choice0: It raises an error at definition time
choice2: The same list is reused by every call, so changes accumulate
choice3: It silently converts the list to a tuple

description: What does *args collect in a function definition?
explanation: *args gathers any extra positional arguments into a tuple.
choice0: Extra positional arguments, as a tuple
choice1: Extra keyword arguments, as a dictionary
choice3: The return values of the function

description: What does **kwargs collect in a function definition?
explanation: **kwargs gathers any extra keyword arguments into a dictionary keyed by argument name.
choice0: Extra positional arguments, as a list
choice1: Extra keyword arguments, as a dictionary
choice3: The functions type annotations

description: What is a lambda in Python?
explanation: A lambda is a small anonymous function written inline, limited to a single expression.
choice0: A loop that runs exactly once
choice1: A way to import a module lazily
choice3: A short anonymous function of one expression

description: What does sorted(words, key=len) do?
explanation: The key function is applied to each item, and the results decide the order, so words are ordered by length.
choice1: Sorts only words of the same length
choice2: Sorts the words from shortest to longest
choice3: Returns the length of each word

description: How do you sort a list from largest to smallest?
explanation: Pass reverse=True to sorted() or sort() to flip the ordering.
choice3: sorted(items, order="desc")

description: What does sorted() do to the list you pass it?
explanation: sorted() leaves the original untouched and returns a new sorted list.
choice0: Sorts it in place and returns None
choice1: Leaves it unchanged and returns a new list
choice2: Sorts it in place and returns it
choice3: Removes duplicates while sorting

description: What does the global keyword do inside a function?
explanation: It tells Python that assignments to that name should change the module-level variable rather than create a local one.
choice0: Lets the function assign to a module-level variable
choice1: Makes a local variable visible to other functions automatically
choice2: Imports a variable from another module
choice3: Prevents the variable from ever changing

description: Why can a function read a module-level variable without declaring anything?
explanation: Name lookup falls back to enclosing and global scopes when a name is not local. Only assignment requires the global keyword.
choice0: Because all variables in Python are global
choice1: Because functions copy all outer variables when defined
choice2: Because name lookup falls back to the enclosing and global scopes
choice3: Because reading a variable creates a local copy of it

description: What does the finally block of a try statement guarantee?
explanation: finally runs whether or not an exception was raised, which makes it the right place for cleanup.
choice0: It runs only when no error occurred
choice1: It runs whether or not an error occurred
choice2: It runs only when an error occurred
choice3: It suppresses any error that was raised

description: Why is except Exception preferred over a bare except?
explanation: A bare except also catches control-flow exceptions such as KeyboardInterrupt, making a program hard to stop or debug.
choice0: A bare except also swallows interrupts and system-exit signals
choice1: A bare except is a syntax error in Python 3
choice2: A bare except is slower to execute
choice3: A bare except cannot be followed by finally

description: What does raise ValueError("bad input") do?
explanation: raise deliberately triggers an exception, which propagates until something catches it.
choice2: Converts the message into a return value
choice3: Raises an exception that stops normal execution

description: What does d.get("k", 0) return when the key k is missing?
explanation: The second argument to get() is the fallback returned when the key is absent, here 0.
choice3: An empty string

description: What does d.setdefault("k", []) do?
explanation: It returns the existing value for the key, or inserts the default and returns that when the key is missing.
choice0: Returns the value, inserting the default first if the key is missing
choice1: Always overwrites the key with an empty list
choice2: Removes the key if it holds an empty list
choice3: Checks whether the key exists without changing anything

description: How can you loop over a dictionary getting both keys and values?
explanation: items() yields key and value pairs, which unpack neatly into two loop variables.
choice3: for k, v in d.keys()

description: What does {**a, **b} produce when a and b are dictionaries?
explanation: It merges them into a new dictionary, with keys from b winning any conflicts.
choice2: An error, because dictionaries cannot be unpacked
choice3: A merged dictionary where b wins on duplicate keys

description: What does {1, 2, 3} & {2, 3, 4} evaluate to?
explanation: The & operator on sets gives the intersection, the items present in both.

description: What does {1, 2, 3} - {2} evaluate to?
explanation: Subtracting sets gives the difference, the items in the first that are not in the second.

description: Why is checking membership in a set usually faster than in a list?
explanation: A set is hash-based, so lookups take roughly constant time. A list must be scanned item by item.
choice0: Sets are always shorter than lists
choice1: Sets use hashing, so lookup does not scan every item
choice2: Sets are stored in sorted order and binary-searched
choice3: Sets keep an index of the last item found

description: What does a, b = b, a do?
explanation: The right side is built as a tuple first, then unpacked, so the two variables swap values in one step.
choice0: Swaps the values of a and b
choice1: Sets both a and b to b
choice3: Creates a tuple named a

description: Why can a tuple be used as a dictionary key when a list cannot?
explanation: Dictionary keys must be hashable, which requires immutability. Tuples are immutable, lists are not.
choice2: Tuples are immutable and therefore hashable
choice3: Lists are stored outside the dictionary

description: What does "a,b,,c".split(",") return?
explanation: split() creates an entry for every separator, so the empty field between the two commas becomes an empty string.

description: Why are strings described as immutable in Python?
explanation: You cannot change a character in place. Methods such as replace() return a new string and leave the original alone.
choice0: Their contents cannot change; methods return new strings
choice1: They cannot be passed to functions
choice3: They cannot be stored in lists

description: What does "Total: {}".format(7) produce?
explanation: format() substitutes its arguments into the braces, giving "Total: 7".
choice3: An error

description: What is the practical difference between range(1000000) and a list of the same numbers?
explanation: range produces values on demand and stores only its bounds, so it uses a fixed small amount of memory.
choice0: There is none; range builds a list internally
choice2: range generates values on demand instead of storing them all
choice3: range can only be looped over once

description: What does a generator expression such as (x * x for x in nums) give you?
explanation: It produces values lazily one at a time rather than building the whole sequence in memory.
choice0: An object that yields values one at a time
choice3: A function that must be called to run

description: What happens if you loop over the same generator twice?
explanation: A generator is exhausted after one pass, so the second loop sees nothing.
choice1: The second loop produces no items
choice3: It doubles every value

description: What does the yield keyword do in a function?
explanation: yield turns the function into a generator, producing a value and pausing until the next one is requested.
choice3: Produces a value and suspends the function until the next request

description: What does [1, 2] == [1, 2] evaluate to, and why?
explanation: Lists compare element by element, so two lists with equal contents are equal even though they are different objects.
choice1: False, because they are different objects
choice3: It raises a TypeError

description: What does "10" < "9" evaluate to?
explanation: Comparing strings works character by character. The character 1 comes before 9, so "10" is considered smaller.
choice2: True, because it compares text character by character
choice3: False, because the lengths differ

description: What does the walrus operator := do?
explanation: It assigns a value and produces it at the same time, so a name can be bound inside an expression such as a while condition.
choice1: Assigns a value inside an expression and returns it
choice3: Unpacks a tuple into variables

description: Why is the with statement preferred for opening files?
explanation: A with block closes the file automatically when it exits, even if an error is raised inside.
choice0: It closes the file automatically, even on error
choice2: It allows two files to share one handle
choice3: It converts the file contents to a list

description: What does opening a file in mode "w" do to an existing file?
explanation: Mode w truncates the file to nothing before writing. Use mode a to add to the end instead.
choice0: Adds new content at the end
choice1: Raises an error because the file exists
choice3: Opens it read-only

description: What is the purpose of the if __name__ == "__main__": guard?
explanation: It runs the block only when the file is executed directly, not when it is imported by another module.
choice0: It defines the entry point of every Python program
choice1: It prevents the file from being imported at all
choice2: It makes the module load faster
choice3: It runs the block only when the file is run directly

description: Roughly how does the time to find an item in an unsorted list grow with its length?
explanation: A scan must check items one by one, so the time grows in proportion to the length of the list.
choice2: In proportion to the square of the length
choice3: It falls as the list grows

description: Which structure is the best choice for repeatedly testing whether a value has been seen before?
explanation: A set gives near-constant-time membership tests, unlike a list which must be scanned.
choice3: A string

description: What is the idiomatic way to check whether a list named items is empty?
explanation: An empty list is falsy, so if not items reads naturally and works for any sequence.
choice0: if len(items) == 0 is the only correct form
choice3: if items.empty()

description: What does the None-safe pattern if value is None test for?
explanation: is None checks identity against the single None object, which is the reliable way to test for absence.
choice0: Whether the variable holds no value at all
choice2: Whether the variable is an empty string
choice3: Whether the variable was ever assigned

description: Why should you avoid modifying a list while looping over it?
explanation: Removing items shifts later positions, so the loop skips elements. Build a new list or iterate over a copy instead.
choice1: The shifting positions cause items to be skipped
choice2: The loop runs twice as many times
choice3: Python silently converts the list to a tuple

description: What does the self parameter refer to in a method?
explanation: self is the particular object the method was called on, giving access to that objects attributes.
choice1: The module the class lives in
choice3: The instance the method was called on

description: When does the __init__ method of a class run?
explanation: __init__ runs automatically right after a new instance is created, to set up its starting state.
choice0: When a new instance is created
choice3: Every time any method is called

description: What is the difference between a class and an instance?
explanation: A class is the template describing structure and behaviour; an instance is one concrete object built from it.
choice0: They are two words for the same thing
choice1: A class is created from an instance
choice2: A class is the template, an instance is one object built from it
choice3: A class holds data, an instance holds only methods

description: What does PEP 8 recommend for indentation?
explanation: PEP 8 asks for four spaces per indentation level and advises against mixing tabs and spaces.
choice3: Eight spaces

description: Which name follows PEP 8 for a normal function?
explanation: PEP 8 uses lower case with underscores for functions and variables, reserving CapWords for class names.
choice3: CALCULATE_TOTAL
